--- title: "Module 1.3: Plan Study Scope by Goal" slug: prerequisites/philosophy-design/module-1.3-what-we-dont-cover sidebar: order: 4 revision_pending: false --- > **Complexity**: `[MEDIUM]` - Long-form module for setting expectations > > **Time to Complete**: 80–110 minutes (author's planning estimate for reading and exercise) > > **Prerequisites**: Module 1.1, Module 1.2 --- ## Learning Outcomes After this module, you will be able to: - **Evaluate** certification study materials by separating exam scope from post-exam specialization. - **Compare** a resource's task and depth with the chosen exam's objectives, including named tools and interfaces. - **Design** a time-boxed learning plan that protects core Kubernetes practice from scope creep. - **Diagnose** scope creep when team pressure, curiosity, or production tooling pulls you away from the exam. - **Implement** a personal boundary that retains required practice and gives unrelated depth a separate learning goal. --- ## Why This Module Matters Hypothetical scenario: a platform team is preparing three engineers for Kubernetes certification. Its production environment includes a managed cloud platform, a service mesh, GitOps delivery, cloud identity integration, and monitoring dashboards. The team proposes a study plan that mirrors those tools. Before adopting it, compare each activity with the published objectives for the intended certification. Provider onboarding may be necessary for work while leaving a workload, networking, or troubleshooting objective without practice; record that gap rather than assuming every Kubernetes-related activity serves the same goal. That scenario asks you to inspect what a study plan leaves unpracticed. Reading about etcd quorum, eBPF datapaths, CNI plugin design, GitOps sync waves or cloud identity can serve a useful goal, but a resource's subject alone does not establish coverage of an exam objective. Record the intended task and the evidence it produces. Certification preparation and workplace specialization can then share relevant context without being treated as interchangeable learning goals or measured improvements in exam performance. This module offers a planning boundary for certification study alongside work and other learning goals. Decide which activities practice the selected objectives, which supply necessary context, and which serve a separate purpose. Work obligations may require specialization before an exam; record that choice and any displaced practice. --- ## Our Philosophy: Exam-Focused, Not Exhaustive For certification study, choose a bounded route through KubeDojo's wider curriculum. Start with the [official CNCF curriculum for your exam](https://github.com/cncf/curriculum), then map each objective to an activity and a result you can check. Related material can provide supporting context or belong in a separate work-learning plan. This is a planning method, not a measured claim that a fixed fraction of topics accounts for a fixed fraction of the exam or guarantees a pass. ```mermaid flowchart LR Topic[Study topic] --> Match{Named exam objective?} Match -->|Yes| Practice[Practice and verify that objective] Match -->|No| Context{Needed to explain an objective?} Context -->|Yes| Support[Bound the supporting context] Context -->|No| Later[Separate work or specialization plan] ``` The diagram classifies study activities; it does not predict question frequency or score. An objective can name a tool or extension mechanism as well as a native object. For example, the [CKA curriculum](https://github.com/cncf/curriculum/blob/bad74bf40372cdb6fb93f0eb1a6758b59b5a2909/CKA_Curriculum_v1.37.pdf) explicitly includes Helm and Kustomize for installing cluster components, plus understanding CRDs and installing and configuring operators. Classifying all third-party tools as out of scope would therefore produce an incomplete plan. Check the intended task and depth before deciding what to defer. Think of a driving test as an analogy for selecting practice: an operating task and designing a vehicle call for different depth. The analogy stops there: a Kubernetes curriculum can explicitly name tools, interfaces and implementation tasks, and it does not establish what any particular exam question will ask. Use the selected exam's actual objectives to decide the depth. KubeDojo's exam-track pin remains Kubernetes 1.35; its separate Release Radar includes other minors. Check the [Linux Foundation exam-environment FAQ](https://docs.linuxfoundation.org/tc-docs/certification/faq-cka-ckad-cks#what-application-version-is-running-in-the-exam-environment) before timed preparation. As checked on October 27, 2026, it lists CKA/CKAD 1.37 and CKS 1.35. The existing pin is not proof of current exam parity. We write the full `kubectl` command so examples do not require a local alias; server queries still require an appropriate configured cluster and permissions. ```bash kubectl version --client kubectl get pods --all-namespaces kubectl auth can-i list pods --all-namespaces ``` **Pause and predict:** compare an evening practicing `kubectl describe`, `kubectl logs`, `kubectl auth can-i` and events with an evening reading a provider's managed node group guide. Which named exam objective or workplace responsibility would each activity practice, and what result would you inspect?
Check your prediction For a chosen exam, map each activity to its actual objective and expected result. A provider guide may also serve a workplace goal; its title alone does not establish either match.
Write the goal and a checkable result for each evening before you continue. The next paragraph is about the discomfort of a narrow curriculum. It does not pick the evening. A focused certification route and production onboarding have different goals, although they may share tasks. Check the chosen route for gaps against the current objectives, and use role-specific sources whenever work requires that depth. --- ## Plan Scope by Goal Classify the actual task rather than treating every adjacent topic as equally urgent or automatically excluded. These are planning boundaries for a selected certification goal, not a list of topics absent from KubeDojo. The checked curricula name native APIs, operational and application tasks, security controls, tools and interfaces at different depths. The categories below help separate additional specialization from required practice. Check the specific objective before deferring a resource, especially when the same product supports both a named task and a much wider feature set. ### Cloud Provider Specifics | Topic | Planning boundary to check | Where to Learn | |-------|-------------|----------------| | AWS EKS details | Compare the actual task with the chosen objective and environment | [EKS Architecture](/cloud/eks-deep-dive/module-5.1-eks-architecture/); AWS and eksctl documentation | | GKE features | Separate the resource's task from additional provider features | [GKE Networking](/cloud/gke-deep-dive/module-6.2-gke-networking/); Google Cloud documentation | | AKS specifics | Check the task and its verification against the chosen objective | [AKS Networking](/cloud/aks-deep-dive/module-7.2-aks-networking/); Azure documentation | | Cloud IAM integration | Map the identity task and its depth before deferring it | [Cloud IAM Integration](/cloud/architecture-patterns/module-4.3-cloud-iam/); provider documentation | For a provider resource, inspect its identity, networking and cluster-operation assumptions. Identify the Kubernetes task and any provider-specific steps, then compare both with the chosen curriculum and environment. A provider workflow may serve a work obligation even when its relation to an exam objective needs further investigation. Record the actual steps rather than inferring coverage from the service's name. For example, compare a cloud load balancer annotation with the purpose of a Service of type `LoadBalancer`, or compare a cloud identity workflow with ServiceAccounts and RBAC. Use provider documentation for its specific integration and record which part, if any, supports the chosen exam task. KubeDojo has other learning tracks as well as certification routes. ### Production Operations at Scale | Topic | Planning boundary to check | Where to Learn | |-------|-------------|----------------| | Multi-cluster federation | Compare the proposed task with the chosen objective | [Multi-Cluster Architecture](/cloud/architecture-patterns/module-4.2-multi-cluster/); project-specific documentation | | Cluster autoscaling | Compare node provisioning with workload replica scaling and the chosen objective | [Karpenter](/platform/toolkits/developer-experience/scaling-reliability/module-6.1-karpenter/); Cluster Autoscaler and provider documentation | | Organization-wide disaster recovery design | Separate service requirements from named exam tasks | [Kubernetes Disaster Recovery](/cloud/advanced-operations/module-8.5-disaster-recovery/); SRE books and company runbooks | | Cost optimization | Identify the cost model, system requirements and intended task | [Cloud Cost Optimization](/cloud/advanced-operations/module-8.8-cloud-cost/); FinOps resources and cloud calculators | For a production-planning activity, write down its operating context. A recovery exercise might ask about data stores, recovery objectives, backup tooling and incident roles. A cost investigation might inspect billing, capacity policies and business priorities. A multi-cluster proposal might examine latency, tenancy, traffic management and operating permissions. These are suggested questions, not a complete design checklist or evidence that a particular system meets its requirements. Inspect the actual resource and local acceptance criteria before assigning depth; retain any task that also maps to the chosen exam objective. Choose the operational task from the curriculum you actually intend to study. The checked CKA curriculum includes preparing cluster infrastructure, creating and managing clusters with kubeadm, managing their lifecycle and implementing and configuring a highly available control plane. A full organizational recovery program adds service-specific responsibilities, but that distinction does not remove the named control-plane task. Map a proposed backup or recovery exercise to the chosen objective and state what it verifies; do not assume the same task is required by CKA, CKAD and CKS. ### Deep Networking | Topic | Depth boundary to check | Where to Learn | |-------|-------------|----------------| | BGP configuration | Compare the configuration task with the chosen objective | [BGP and Core Routing](/platform/foundations/advanced-networking/module-1.4-bgp-routing/); network engineering resources | | Service mesh internals | Retain the CKS encryption task naming Istio; classify other mesh depth separately | [Service Mesh](/platform/toolkits/infrastructure-networking/networking/module-5.2-service-mesh/); project documentation | | eBPF/Cilium internals | Retain the CKS encryption task naming Cilium; classify unrelated datapath internals separately | [Cilium](/platform/toolkits/infrastructure-networking/networking/module-5.1-cilium/); Cilium documentation | | Custom CNI development | Distinguish plugin authorship from the CKA interface objective | [CNI and Cluster Networking](/k8s/cka/part3-services-networking/module-3.7-cni/); CNI specification for plugin authorship | For a networking resource, identify the task it supports before choosing its depth. A Service connectivity exercise can involve labels, selectors, ports, endpoints, DNS, NetworkPolicy and troubleshooting. An implementation guide may address a different objective or additional specialization. Those connections do not establish one networking syllabus for every certification; compare the exact activity with the chosen curriculum and record how you will verify its result. The distinction matters during practice. If a NetworkPolicy blocks traffic, inspect labels, selectors, rules and the intended source and destination. The checked CKA curriculum's cluster-architecture domain explicitly names understanding extension interfaces such as CNI, CSI and CRI. Plugin authorship is a different activity from understanding an interface or implementing the named task. A product name alone cannot decide whether a resource belongs in the plan: the checked CKS curriculum names Cilium and Istio for Pod-to-Pod encryption. ### Specific Tools and Projects | Tool | Depth boundary to check | Where to Learn | |------|-------------|----------------| | ArgoCD | Separate tool-specific sync workflows from the chosen objective | [ArgoCD](/platform/toolkits/cicd-delivery/gitops-deployments/module-2.1-argocd/); ArgoCD documentation | | Istio | Retain the named CKS encryption task; classify other features separately | [Service Mesh](/platform/toolkits/infrastructure-networking/networking/module-5.2-service-mesh/); Istio documentation | | Terraform | Separate infrastructure provisioning from the named Kubernetes task | [Terraform](/platform/toolkits/infrastructure-networking/iac-tools/module-7.1-terraform/); HashiCorp Learn | | Prometheus/Grafana | Map the proposed monitoring activity to the exact objective | [Prometheus](/platform/toolkits/observability-intelligence/observability/module-1.1-prometheus/) and [Grafana](/platform/toolkits/observability-intelligence/observability/module-1.3-grafana/); project documentation | Separate a product's full curriculum from the specific task a certification names. The checked [CKS curriculum](https://github.com/cncf/curriculum/blob/bad74bf40372cdb6fb93f0eb1a6758b59b5a2909/CKS_Curriculum%20v1.34.pdf), Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities, names Cilium and Istio for implementing Pod-to-Pod encryption. Blanket advice to postpone both products would therefore omit relevant CKS practice. Record the required behavior, the environment and how you will verify it, then classify unrelated features deliberately; the outline does not describe the products' entire feature sets. This retrieved curriculum file is named v1.34; the separately checked FAQ lists the CKS exam environment as 1.35. A curriculum-file label and an exam runtime are distinct evidence, so recheck both before preparation. Helm is explicit in both the [CKA](https://github.com/cncf/curriculum/blob/bad74bf40372cdb6fb93f0eb1a6758b59b5a2909/CKA_Curriculum_v1.37.pdf) and [CKAD](https://github.com/cncf/curriculum/blob/bad74bf40372cdb6fb93f0eb1a6758b59b5a2909/CKAD_Curriculum_v1.37.pdf) curricula checked on October 27, 2026. CKA names Helm and Kustomize for installing cluster components; CKAD names deploying existing packages with Helm. Practice the named tasks rather than treating Helm as either universally optional or a reason to master every chart-authoring workflow. Apply the same objective-by-objective check to your chosen exam instead of transferring exclusions from another certification. Worked planning example: suppose your bookmark list contains a Helm chart-authoring course, a lab that deploys an existing package with Helm, and a guide to installing a cluster component. Write the exact objective beside each resource before assigning study time. For the checked CKAD curriculum, verify that the lab actually uses the Helm package manager to deploy an existing package before classifying it under that objective. For CKA, the objective names Helm and Kustomize for installing cluster components; inspect which tasks the guide practices and what remains uncovered. A resource's title alone does not establish that all its material is required by either objective. Now write the evidence you would want from the selected lab: identify the package and target environment, explain the configuration you selected, inspect the deployed resources, and verify the intended result. Record any setup or permissions the lab assumes. This is a hypothetical plan, not an observed installation or proof of exam readiness. If you cannot explain which objective the exercise demonstrates, investigate that gap before labeling the resource essential. The method preserves relevant tool practice while giving additional chart-development material a deliberate place in the wider learning plan. **Pause and predict:** if your company uses Istio heavily, should you study it for the CKA?
Check your prediction Learn enough at work to avoid being dangerous in production. Do not spend certification study blocks on service mesh internals unless your immediate goal has changed. Name the goal of each study session before you start.
Write yes or no, and which hours you would use, before you continue. The next section explains how to choose study depth for a particular goal. It does not answer the Istio question. --- ## Why We Make These Choices One reason is to allocate limited study time deliberately. A plan can reserve sessions for named tasks and their verification while recording other goals separately. Practice might include reading manifests, inspecting events, or fixing a configuration when those activities support the chosen objective; this is a planning recommendation, not a measured speed or pass-rate claim. ```mermaid flowchart LR Plan[Study plan] --> Objectives[Map resources to named objectives] Objectives --> Practice[Perform the intended tasks] Practice --> Inspect[Inspect results and remaining gaps] Inspect --> Plan ``` The second reason is exam relevance. CKA, CKAD and CKS have separate published curricula; use the exact objective as the planning reference rather than assuming a shared native-only syllabus. A KubeDojo route still needs verification against that objective and the current environment. Record a concrete gap when a route omits required practice, and give unrelated material a separate learning goal. Popularity in production does not establish an exam requirement, and a third-party name does not establish an exclusion. The third reason is maintainability. Review each route for version drift, deprecated behavior, changed defaults, and objective updates. Additional topics create additional material to check; this is a maintenance consideration, not a measured relationship between breadth and error rates. Compare the stated target with current provider requirements and versioned technical sources; a narrow scope alone does not establish that its content is current. Record the date and unresolved differences beside the plan rather than assuming a familiar resource still matches it. Use the required action as a check on the resource you choose. Reading a broad product tour and implementing a named task produce different evidence. For a NetworkPolicy exercise, write the intended traffic rule and test its result; for an encryption objective, identify and verify the required behavior. Do not infer question frequency or a universal backup requirement from those examples. The three captured outlines do not explicitly name an etcd snapshot-and-restore workflow; classify such practice against the selected cluster objective and environment instead of asserting that every exam rewards it. Before another study session, name the expected output and the objective it supports. A corrected manifest or explained troubleshooting result can provide evidence of the particular task practiced; a bookmark alone does not demonstrate that task. Neither result proves exam readiness by itself. --- ## The "Just Enough" Principle "Just enough" does not mean shallow. Match depth to the chosen task and its verification. For example, the checked CKA outline names implementing and configuring a highly available control plane, while CKAD names application deployments and health checks. Keep that distinction when planning practice. A production recovery plan also needs service-specific dependencies, validation and operating responsibilities; a cluster exercise alone does not establish that complete plan. Do not use the depth of the broader topic to exclude a task the curriculum actually names. ```mermaid flowchart TD Goal[Name the goal and target environment] --> Task[Define the task and its verification] Task --> Exam[Certification: map to the published objective] Task --> Work[Production: identify dependencies and recovery requirements] Exam --> Gap[Record missing knowledge or practice] Work --> Gap ``` **Pause and predict:** why does a successful backup command alone leave unanswered questions about recovery of a production service?
Check your prediction A command result does not establish whether the service's data dependencies, recovery procedure, access requirements, and acceptable recovery time have been tested together. Identify what the chosen exam objective requires separately from what the actual service needs. The diagram assigns no numerical difficulty, study hours, or relative importance to either goal.
Write the missing recovery evidence before you continue. Then compare it with the bounded task in your chosen curriculum; keep the scope and verification criteria explicit for each goal. This principle also helps you avoid false equivalence. NetworkPolicy practice requires inspecting selectors and testing intended traffic, while enforcement depends on a network plugin that supports it. HPA adjusts a workload's replica count using metrics; Cluster Autoscaler adjusts node capacity through supported infrastructure. Compare the actual task and depth with the selected objective instead of inferring an exclusion or question frequency from either mechanism. A useful study question is not "Could this ever matter?" Ask which part of the resource serves the named objective and which part adds another learning goal. Retain required practice even when it uses a specific tool or needs substantial work. Give unrelated depth a separate plan with an explicit reason; the resource's size or vendor-specific label alone does not establish that it belongs after the exam. Hypothetical planning example: a Service exercise checks selectors, endpoints and ports, while a provider guide explains controller annotations and cost. Record the objective and expected result for the first activity and the workplace purpose for the second; inspect each resource before deciding whether any part also supports the selected exam. --- ## Where We Suggest Going Deeper Specialization can run alongside or follow certification study, depending on your work and learning goals. A platform engineer, application developer, security engineer and SRE may choose different areas of depth. The following paths are examples to investigate, not a required sequence or a claim about exam outcomes. For platform engineers, a possible separate goal is platform design: evaluate Cluster API, GitOps with ArgoCD or Flux, multi-tenancy patterns, developer portals, or policy controls against a particular team's requirements. Ask about ownership, upgrade paths, tenancy, and how much Kubernetes detail to expose to users. Treat these as candidate study activities, with project documentation and a defined verification task for each. A certification record alone does not establish that a proposed internal product meets its users' needs. For developers, a possible goal is application architecture on Kubernetes. Compare a sidecar, ambassador, or adapter exercise with the application behavior you intend to study. Before choosing operator, CRD, plugin, or client development, record the relevant API and reconciliation assumptions and what normal workload objects already provide. Then define a check for the proposed extension's behavior and failure handling. This is suggested preparation, not evidence that a learning sequence makes software safer or that every developer needs these activities. For security-focused learners, candidate activities include policy authoring, runtime detection, supply chain verification, NetworkPolicy design, admission control, and threat modeling for a stated environment. Inspect project documentation before choosing a tool-specific exercise. Compare its actual task with the CKS objectives before calling it post-exam material. Separately record the system's operational controls, logging, incident-response responsibilities, and evidence requirements; an exam objective does not by itself define the complete security acceptance criteria for a production system. For SRE and operations work, consider a separate plan for SLO-based alerting, capacity planning, controlled failure experiments, backup validation, incident response, upgrades, and incident review. Choose activities against the service's requirements and local procedures. Record expected behavior, operating assumptions, failure boundaries, and the evidence still missing. The checked certification curricula name particular tasks; they do not establish that passing an exam verifies all of these service responsibilities or replaces evidence from operating the particular system. Compare two hypothetical plans: one mixes certification tasks and workplace-tool study in each session; the other separates those goals into scheduled blocks. Either plan needs an objective and a result to inspect. Choose based on your available time, current gaps and work obligations, then review what the sessions actually covered. This is planning advice, not evidence that one schedule produces faster certification or a particular pass rate. --- ## Visualization: KubeDojo Scope The scope diagram distinguishes two learning goals. A certification plan follows its named objectives; a workplace plan follows the responsibilities of a particular system. They can share concepts and practice, but neither is a complete substitute for the other. KubeDojo also has separate cloud, Linux, platform and other learning tracks, so this module's study boundary is not a description of everything the site covers. ```mermaid flowchart TD KubeDojo[KubeDojo learning routes] --> Cert[Certification plan] KubeDojo --> Work[Workplace or specialization plan] Cert --> Objectives[Named exam objectives and practice] Work --> Responsibilities[System requirements and operating responsibilities] Objectives --> Shared[Identify shared concepts and separate gaps] Responsibilities --> Shared ``` Use this diagram when work relevance and exam relevance compete for the same study time. Map the resource to an objective or an operating responsibility and decide which goal has priority now. Keep deferred material visible with its reason and a review date. This records your planning choice without claiming that a tool is universally irrelevant or that a particular allocation guarantees a better score. Use the diagram to justify a decision about a particular ArgoCD or BGP activity, rather than excluding a whole product or topic. An omitted keyword in an outline does not prove a task is forbidden; record uncertainty when the relationship to an objective is unclear. --- ## How to Classify a Topic Before It Steals a Week The most practical skill in this module is classification. When a new topic appears, do not ask whether it is interesting, modern, or used by serious teams, because those questions are too easy to answer with yes. Ask what role the topic plays in your current goal. A topic can be exam scope, supporting context, post-exam specialization, or workplace urgency. Those categories let you make a decision without arguing about whether the topic has value in some abstract sense. For exam-scope topics, practice the action and depth stated by the selected objective. The checked outlines include understanding and knowledge as well as implementation and configuration. Match the evidence accordingly: an explained interface role, a configured workload, or a troubleshooting record answer different tasks. Identify what the artifact demonstrates and what it leaves unverified. A familiar command or an explanation without notes can be a practice result, but neither alone establishes competence across every objective or predicts an exam score. Supporting context helps explain a named task without becoming a separate goal. For example, a mental model of reconciliation can support understanding Deployments, and plugin behavior can explain NetworkPolicy enforcement. Compare a custom-controller or CNI-development activity with the chosen objective before allocating time; the CKA explicitly names understanding extension interfaces. Specialization can preserve a separate learning goal. If an ArgoCD sync-wave activity or Cilium eBPF internals tour does not practice your selected objective or supply needed context, record why you deferred it and when to revisit it. A different activity using the same product may map to an objective, such as CKS Pod-to-Pod encryption. Workplace urgency can override an exam plan consciously. If an on-call responsibility requires a provider incident runbook, record the tradeoff and reschedule displaced exam practice. Inspect the runbook's actual tasks before deciding whether any also support a CKA objective. A useful classification habit is to write one sentence before opening any long resource: "I am reading this because it will help me do X for this published objective." Fill in X with the named task, including a tool or interface when specified. Then identify the evidence you expect to produce. If the connection is missing, investigate it before assigning study time; a product name, a native object or an advanced label is not the scope decision. ### Worked classifications before you plan The following are **authored hypothetical resource cards**, not published courses or executed labs. They show planning decisions using page 2 of the linked curricula at revision `bad74bf`; the evidence described is expected or still missing, never an observed installation or result. The categories are provisional: inspecting an actual resource could change any decision. **Card 1 — CKA availability and interfaces.** The Cluster Architecture, Installation and Configuration objectives distinguish activities: implement and configure a highly available control plane, and understand extension interfaces such as CNI, CSI and CRI. Imagine a resource whose stated activity is to configure a highly available control plane and check whether the control plane remains usable when a component is unavailable. Place that activity in `Exam Scope` provisionally: its intended task maps to the availability objective. The planned evidence is a description of the configuration and an availability check with its assumptions and result recorded. No such check has been performed here, and the outline does not specify that this hypothetical check is the exam's marking scheme. Now imagine a second resource that explains where CNI, CSI and CRI fit and asks the reader to explain their roles. Map that activity to the separate interface objective; record the explanation as its expected evidence. A third resource teaches writing a plugin from scratch. Its extra development depth does not by itself demonstrate either interface understanding or control-plane availability, so place that activity in a separate goal unless inspection shows a relevant component. Revisit if its actual exercise includes the interface explanation or if the selected objective changes. None of these descriptions establishes that a single-control-plane lab satisfies the availability task. **Card 2 — CKAD existing packages.** Application Deployment names using the Helm package manager to deploy existing packages. Imagine an activity that selects an existing package and deploys it with Helm in a stated environment. Record the objective's verb and tool, the package and configuration the activity actually uses, and the expected evidence: a deployment result, an inspection of its resources, and a check of the intended package behavior. Record which behavior that check covers and what remains unverified. The planned classification is `Exam Scope` because the described task maps to that objective; the actual resource, environment, permissions and outcome remain unverified. A list of Helm commands, a chart title, or resource presence alone would not establish that the intended behavior works. Contrast an imagined tutorial devoted to authoring a new chart. Record its actual authoring task and defer that extra depth to a separate goal if it does not also practice deploying an existing package. The revisit condition is discovery of a relevant deployment activity or a changed objective, not a conclusion that chart authoring is forbidden. Transfer the same resource to CKA only after checking its task: CKA names using Helm and Kustomize to install cluster components. A CKAD application-package activity does not automatically demonstrate that CKA component-installation task, even though both mention Helm. **Card 3 — CKS encryption.** Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities names implementing Pod-to-Pod encryption (Cilium, Istio). Imagine an activity that practices encryption using Cilium. Mark the described activity provisionally `Exam Scope` and inspect whether it covers the named objective and what remains to be practiced, including the other named tool; do not infer full coverage from one activity. Plan evidence that identifies the communicating Pods, the tool and the check used to distinguish encrypted from unencrypted traffic. Record the expected result and the limits of that check; this card reports no setup, traffic capture or observed encryption. A general mesh traffic-routing tour or an eBPF internals overview is a different actual activity. Classify its relevant context separately, and defer unrelated depth with a reason and a condition to revisit after inspecting the resource. **Version and uncertainty record.** The captured CKA and CKAD curriculum files are labeled v1.37, while the captured CKS curriculum file is labeled v1.34. The separately checked FAQ on October 27, 2026 lists CKA/CKAD runtime 1.37 and CKS runtime 1.35. For CKS, record this label/runtime mismatch and recheck both sources and the intended resource's compatibility before scheduling the exercise; the mismatch does not prove either that the objective is absent or that a particular resource works. Do the same for other exams when versions or objectives change. A provisional map is a planning artifact, not evidence of completion, compatibility or a future question. Consider a learner who asks why one Pod cannot reach another. Define the intended traffic and inspect the relevant objects and events. For CKA, retain the named extension-interface and networking work. For CKS, retain the named encryption task rather than filing every Cilium resource under specialization. An unrelated implementation tour can belong in a separate plan, while a live production incident follows its local runbook. The symptom alone does not determine which depth serves the selected objective. Apply the same classification to security. Example RBAC practice can include Roles and RoleBindings, permission checks with `kubectl auth can-i`, and explanations of namespace-scoped versus cluster-scoped grants; select the depth from the chosen objective. ServiceAccounts provide identities for processes in Pods. Inspect policy authoring, admission control, workload identity, or signing activities individually before assigning a category. A work obligation may also require an emergency-access procedure independently of the exam plan; record that purpose and any assumptions it makes. Classification can help you notice when an interesting advanced topic has displaced a named task. For example, compare a service mesh architecture reading with a Service selector troubleshooting exercise: record what each activity demonstrates against the chosen objective before assigning study time. This comparison does not rank candidates or predict exam performance. Check the opposite planning error too: an activity without a demonstrated exam match can still serve a work or personal goal. Record that separate purpose instead of treating it as worthless. "This is worth investigating later" should include a reason and a revisit condition. For example, a provider-controller topic might return to the active plan when a new work responsibility requires it. This is a suggested planning habit, not a claim about learner health or later production performance. When you classify a resource, also classify the expected output. Exam-scope work should end in practice results, such as solved labs or commands you can repeat. Supporting context can end in a short explanation or a diagram. Post-exam specialization can end in a bookmark plus a reason to return. Workplace urgency can end in a runbook note or an incident action. If every category ends in the same pile of notes, you have not really made a decision. A boundary can be a queue rather than a rejection of curiosity. Order activities by the immediate goal, retain their separate purposes, and revisit the order when an objective, resource, or work obligation changes. The queue records a choice; it does not establish competence or predict workplace outcomes. --- ## When This Doesn't Apply When preparing for a certification, try this classification as a planning aid, particularly when a date or study hours are constrained. A team can use the same labels to discuss scope, while retaining a separate workplace goal where necessary. KubeDojo also offers routes for goals beyond certification. The anti-pattern is equally simple: do not use an exam-focused path as your only production training plan. If you are on call for a real cluster tomorrow, you may need provider-specific runbooks, company incident procedures, backup validation, dashboards, logging conventions, and tool-specific safety checks before you finish a certification track. Exam focus is not an excuse to ignore operational risk. It is a way to keep one learning goal from swallowing another. Keep curiosity visible in the plan. Capture a separate topic with its source, why it matters, and a condition for revisiting it; if it becomes urgent for work, adjust the schedule explicitly rather than assuming it practices the exam task. Here is a worked example you can reuse when a team study group starts drifting. Imagine the group is preparing for the CKA and one member suggests a session on managed cloud load balancer annotations because their production ingress depends on them. The facilitator should not argue that annotations are useless. Instead, they should ask what native task the session improves. If the answer is "understanding Services," the group can spend ten minutes explaining the provider layer, then return to Service types, selectors, endpoints, ports, and troubleshooting. If the answer is "learning our cloud platform," the session belongs in a separate workplace track. Suppose someone proposes replacing an RBAC drill with a policy-engine deep dive for a workplace adoption. Compare each activity with the chosen exam's security objectives and identify its expected result. Record the work goal separately, retain any required exam practice, and revisit the classification if the resource contains a relevant named task. In a hypothetical group, a senior colleague may recommend a topic from an incident while another learner hesitates to question it. Ask what that resource would demonstrate and whether its task also serves the selected objective. One possible response is: "What result would we check, and which goal does it serve?" Record the incident context without inventing it, preserve any work obligation, and reschedule displaced practice explicitly. This example does not establish how frequently such conversations occur or which wording changes learning outcomes. Try the boundary when studying alone: inspect several open resources and write the actual activity, selected objective, and expected result for each. A resource might remain supporting context, move to a separate goal, or need further inspection. Explain the decision before closing or moving it, and keep a revisit condition where useful. This exercise is intended to make the allocation visible; moving a tab does not demonstrate that the selected practice happened or that study time became more effective. You can record temporary incompleteness explicitly: "I do not yet know this provider controller's internals; I will check the object it watches and the symptom before deciding what to study next." This makes the uncertainty and next action visible without claiming expertise. --- ## When You'd Use This vs Alternatives Use this certification-goal boundary when planning exam practice. KubeDojo also has lessons for provider operations, tools, networking and reliability. Combine relevant lessons with vendor and project documentation, SRE books, company runbooks, or incident reviews when the goal calls for their specific context. These resources answer different questions. | Learning Goal | Starting Resources | Why These Sources Fit | |---------------|---------------------|----------------------| | Prepare for a chosen certification | Official curriculum and environment requirements, plus a checked KubeDojo route | Map the exact tasks and identify gaps; this packet checks CKA, CKAD and CKS outlines, not every certification. | | Operate EKS, GKE, or AKS | [EKS Architecture](/cloud/eks-deep-dive/module-5.1-eks-architecture/), [GKE Networking](/cloud/gke-deep-dive/module-6.2-gke-networking/), [AKS Networking](/cloud/aks-deep-dive/module-7.2-aks-networking/), [Cloud IAM](/cloud/architecture-patterns/module-4.3-cloud-iam/), provider documentation and company runbooks | Check the specific service's identity, upgrades, networking, storage, and support boundaries. | | Adopt ArgoCD, Istio, Terraform, or Prometheus | [ArgoCD](/platform/toolkits/cicd-delivery/gitops-deployments/module-2.1-argocd/), [Service Mesh](/platform/toolkits/infrastructure-networking/networking/module-5.2-service-mesh/), [Terraform](/platform/toolkits/infrastructure-networking/iac-tools/module-7.1-terraform/), [Prometheus](/platform/toolkits/observability-intelligence/observability/module-1.1-prometheus/), [Grafana](/platform/toolkits/observability-intelligence/observability/module-1.3-grafana/) and project documentation | Check the selected project's model, commands, assumptions, and failure handling. Recovery](/cloud/advanced-operations/module-8.5-disaster-recovery/), SRE practice and company runbooks | The right answer depends on risk, traffic, data, staffing, and business constraints. | | Investigate scaling and cost | [Karpenter](/platform/toolkits/developer-experience/scaling-reliability/module-6.1-karpenter/), [Cloud Cost Optimization](/cloud/advanced-operations/module-8.8-cloud-cost/) and provider documentation | Compare node provisioning, workload scaling and local cost requirements. | | Explore networking depth | [BGP and Core Routing](/platform/foundations/advanced-networking/module-1.4-bgp-routing/), [Cilium](/platform/toolkits/infrastructure-networking/networking/module-5.1-cilium/), [CNI and Cluster Networking](/k8s/cka/part3-services-networking/module-3.7-cni/) and project documentation | Match the networking task to the goal; plugin authorship may need additional specialist resources. | Name the job before choosing the resource. "Practice the checked CKAD deployment objective," "debug our Istio ingress path," and "investigate cloud spend" need their own expected evidence. Inspect the resource against that stated job rather than assuming that general usefulness establishes a match. Check a KubeDojo route in the same way: record its target, covered activity, verification, and any missing practice. The plan is a proposal to inspect, not proof that a site or resource prepares every learner. --- ## Did You Know? - **CNCF publishes separate exam curricula.** Use the [official curriculum repository](https://github.com/cncf/curriculum) to check the objectives for the certification you intend to take; inclusion in a broader landscape is a different question. - **The checked CKA curriculum includes tools and extension mechanisms.** Its Cluster Architecture, Installation and Configuration domain names Helm, Kustomize, CRDs and operators; native-versus-third-party is therefore insufficient as a scope rule. - **The checked curricula have version labels.** Record the official revision and recheck it before scheduling practice; an old course outline or a coworker's memory is not a substitute for inspecting the selected objectives. - **"Expert" is context-dependent.** A networking expert, security expert, developer platform engineer, and SRE may all be strong at Kubernetes while having different deep specialties. --- ## Common Mistakes When Studying for Kubernetes Certifications | Mistake | Why It Happens | How to Fix It | |---------|----------------|---------------| | **Classifying a network tool by name alone** | Plugin development, interface knowledge and security tasks can appear in adjacent documentation. | Map the task: CKA names extension interfaces; CKS names Cilium/Istio for Pod-to-Pod encryption. Separate those activities from unrelated internals. | | **Memorizing YAML syntax** | A blank editor can encourage memorizing fields without checking their meaning. | Practice `kubectl run` and `kubectl create` with `--dry-run=client -o yaml`, then inspect, edit and verify the generated manifest. | | **Studying cloud-specific IAM** | Your company uses AWS IRSA, EKS Pod Identity, GKE Workload Identity, or AKS integrations, so it feels like core Kubernetes. | Focus first on ServiceAccounts, Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, ClusterRoleBindings, and `kubectl auth can-i` in vanilla Kubernetes. | | **Choosing a lab by hardware alone** | Hands-on hardware can distract from the intended task. | Choose an environment that supports the selected objective and its verification; check its setup and limitations. | | **Treating Helm as universally optional or exhaustive** | A workplace chart workflow can obscure the specific task named in a curriculum. | Practice the Helm tasks named by your exam; both the checked CKA and CKAD curricula include Helm. Keep unrelated chart-authoring depth in a separate plan. | | **Classifying a GitOps guide by name** | A product guide can contain several different activities. | Inspect the sync task and compare it with the chosen objective; record a separate work goal or uncertainty where appropriate. | | **Assuming one etcd study rule fits every exam** | Cluster operation and application development are different goals. | Map the specific task to your exam's objective and environment; distinguish demonstrated cluster mechanics from a complete service recovery plan. | --- ## Quiz
Your manager wants you to spend the next two weeks learning Terraform and EKS because your team uses them in production. How should you protect your CKA study plan? Compare the actual Terraform and EKS activities with the chosen CKA objectives and record the work requirement. Schedule both obligations where possible; if work takes priority, identify and reschedule the named exam practice displaced. The product names alone do not settle the classification.
You are studying NetworkPolicies and find a long Cilium eBPF tutorial that looks excellent. Should it become part of this week's CKAD plan? Inspect the tutorial's actual task and compare it with the checked CKAD objectives. If it only explores eBPF internals and does not practice the selected policy task or needed context, give it a separate goal and plan policy scenarios with predicted and checked traffic. Revisit the decision if the resource contains a relevant task; its Cilium title alone cannot decide it.
Your study calendar gives equal time to ArgoCD setup and standard Deployments and Services. What is wrong with that allocation? Identify the objective each allocation serves. Studying ArgoCD sync behavior does not itself demonstrate the checked curricula's workload, Service or troubleshooting tasks. If the resource does not practice a named objective or supply needed context, give it a separate learning goal and restore the missing task practice. That decision depends on the resource's actual activity; it is not a rule that every third-party product belongs outside certification study.
A colleague failed a practice exam after relying on the AWS Console for node operations at work. How would you diagnose the scope creep in their preparation? The practice result alone does not establish the cause. Compare the missed practice tasks with the CKA objectives and the console walkthrough's actual steps, then plan exercises for any missing tasks and their verification. Keep the managed-service workflow for its work purpose and revisit this diagnosis with more evidence.
You see Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and Cluster Autoscaler in the same documentation session. Which one deserves exam focus, and how do you compare the two? HPA adjusts workload replicas using metrics; Cluster Autoscaler adjusts node capacity through supported infrastructure. Identify the task in each resource and map it to the chosen curriculum and environment, then reserve time for named practice and verification. Neither mechanism nor an omitted keyword proves an exam exclusion or predicts question frequency.
You plan to build a highly available bare-metal cluster with external etcd before taking the CKA next week. Is that a good design for a time-boxed learning plan? Do not defer high availability merely because it sounds advanced: the checked CKA curriculum explicitly includes implementing and configuring a highly available control plane. Break the proposal into that named task and additional hardware or organizational requirements. Choose a lab where you can perform and verify the required task with your available preparation time; park extra complexity with a reason. A single-control-plane lab can serve other objectives, but it does not itself demonstrate this availability objective. The curriculum does not supply a prediction of next week's questions.
You have a bookmark list full of Istio, ArgoCD, Cilium, provider IAM, and etcd articles. How would you implement a personal boundary without losing those resources? Use the exercise's three categories: exam scope, supporting context and post-exam specialization. Classify each resource's actual task against the chosen curriculum. A CKS resource practicing Pod-to-Pod encryption may belong in exam scope even if its title says Istio or Cilium; a tour of unrelated internals can belong elsewhere. For CKA, retain the named control-plane and extension-interface practice. Record why a resource is deferred and what evidence would change the classification. Do not use the presence of a product name as the rule.
--- ## Hands-On Exercise: Audit Your Study Materials This exercise is a planning lab rather than a cluster lab because the skill you need is scope control. Open your current study bookmarks, playlists, notes, company wiki pages, or training backlog. Your job is to turn an unfocused pile of useful resources into a certification plan that has a clear boundary and a separate post-exam roadmap. ### Setup Create a short document with three headings: `Exam Scope`, `Supporting Context`, and `Post-Exam Specialization`. If you already have a study tracker, add those labels there instead of creating a new file. The tool does not matter; the decision quality matters. ### Tasks 1. Inventory at least twelve resources, recording the chosen exam and official curriculum revision and page or section. For each, describe the actual activity and depth after inspecting it, not just its title. 2. Map each activity to the exact objective and expected evidence or result, then assign `Exam Scope`, `Supporting Context`, or `Post-Exam Specialization`. Record uncertainty, any defer reason, and a condition for revisiting the decision; investigate a missing match instead of treating a product name or omitted keyword as proof of exclusion. 3. Compare the advanced items with the native Kubernetes tasks they might be replacing. For example, compare an Istio traffic policy tutorial with Service and NetworkPolicy practice, or compare a cloud IAM guide with RBAC drills. 4. Design a one-week time-boxed learning plan around the named tasks and their verification, including tools or interfaces where specified. Give supporting context and unrelated depth an explicit purpose instead of assuming a native-only time allocation. 5. Diagnose one likely pressure point that could pull you off plan, such as a manager asking for provider knowledge, a coworker recommending a tool, or your own curiosity about internals. 6. Write a boundary sentence naming an activity, its reason, and the condition that would make you revisit it, including a work obligation if applicable.
Hint 1: Concept An objective names an intended task; a product name does not tell you which part of a resource practices it.
Hint 2: Approach Write one row with exam, revision and page, resource task and depth, objective, expected evidence, uncertainty, and revisit condition before classifying it.
Hint 3: Example For CKAD, compare an activity deploying an existing package with Helm to the Application Deployment objective. Inspect the activity before deciding whether it actually provides that practice.
Solution guidance Compare your records with the worked classifications above: each needs an inspected task, objective mapping, expected evidence, uncertainty and a revisit condition. Check whether your chosen resources actually support the planned task, and record missing evidence rather than treating the hypothetical cards as results.
**Card A: Two evenings, one exam next week.** One evening is `kubectl describe`, logs, `auth can-i`, and events. The other is a cloud provider's managed node group guide. A friend says both are "Kubernetes" so they count the same.
Check your prediction For a chosen exam, map the command activities and the guide's actual task to its objectives and expected results. Schedule the missing practice, and retain or defer the guide according to its demonstrated purpose and any work obligation.
**Card B: Istio is the production mesh.** The company runs Istio. The learner's next exam is the CKA. The study block this week is booked for VirtualService internals.
Check your prediction Compare the VirtualService activity with the selected CKA objective and record its workplace purpose. Keep any named tool or interface practice that the objective requires; defer unrelated internals with a reason and revisit condition.
**Card C: A backup command succeeded.** Someone treats that result as proof both of exam readiness and of a production recovery plan.
Check your prediction Failure layer: a command result was substituted for the intended acceptance criteria. Next action: check the published exam objective and identify the service-level recovery evidence still missing. Neither goal follows automatically from that one result.
**Card D: The mesh tutorial replaced the policy drill.** A CKAD plan has an Istio traffic-policy video and no practice for its selected NetworkPolicy objective. The video has not yet been inspected.
Check your prediction Inspect the video's actual task and restore practice for the selected CKAD objective if it is missing. A separate CKS plan must retain its named Pod-to-Pod encryption task (Cilium, Istio); the product name alone cannot classify either resource or establish full coverage.
### Success Criteria - [ ] You have evaluated at least twelve study materials and assigned each one to `Exam Scope`, `Supporting Context`, or `Post-Exam Specialization`. - [ ] Your record names the exam and curriculum revision and page or section, actual resource task and depth, objective mapping, expected evidence or result, uncertainty, and any defer reason and revisit condition. At least two decisions cite exact objectives and retain named tool practice. - [ ] You have compared at least one advanced topic with the native Kubernetes task it was displacing. - [ ] You have designed a one-week time-boxed learning plan that retains the named tasks and their required verification, including specified tools and interfaces. - [ ] You have diagnosed one realistic scope-creep pressure point and written how you will respond. - [ ] You have written a boundary sentence with a reason and a condition for revisiting it. --- ## Sources - > **Complexity**: `[MEDIUM]` - Long-form guidance on what not to learn.
>
> **Time to Complete**: 80–110 minutes (long-form read + hands-on exercise)
>
> **Prerequisites**: Module 1.1, Module 1.2, Module 1.3.

---

## What You'll Be Able to Do

After this module, you will be able to:

- **Evaluate** container orchestration technologies using governance, ecosystem, cloud-provider support, and adoption signals.
- **Diagnose** the difference between formal project retirement and a deployment model that does not meet a workload's requirements.
- **Compare** Docker image-building workflows with Kubernetes runtime integrations before and after built-in dockershim removal.
- **Design** a modernization plan that justifies which tools to retain or replace against documented capabilities and operating requirements.

## Why This Module Matters

Hypothetical scenario: a retailer is reviewing an existing container platform before expanding it. Its engineers need to determine which components remain supported, what happens when a host fails, how application changes are rolled out, and who maintains the integrations. They are considering Kubernetes, but neither a migration nor keeping the current platform is automatically the right answer. The audit needs a dated maintainer record, documented capabilities for the intended version, and tests of the failures the service must tolerate. This scenario supplies decision questions, not a real company's spending, hiring history, incident or measured migration outcome.

The opening scenario asks you to check evidence before selecting a replacement. A dated maintainer record can establish project retirement, while capability documentation describes a deployment model. Neither identifies the requirements of every organization. For a learning or engineering decision, state which product and version you mean, which responsibilities the team must support, and what information is missing. That keeps the audit useful without pretending a tool name determines the answer.

This module examines technologies and deployment choices in relation to Kubernetes. Docker Swarm, Apache Mesos, Cloud Foundry, Chef, Puppet, Ansible, and Docker Compose have different purposes and lifecycle states; their names alone do not determine whether a particular use is obsolete. Practice checking documented status, operational fit, ownership, and missing evidence before proposing a change.

## Start With the Shape of a Dead End

A "dead end" is a question to investigate, not a status supplied by a product name. A project may be formally retired, a supported deployment may fail a particular requirement, or a team may need a different learning goal. Record the exact product and version, the decision being made, and the evidence that would change it. A lifecycle record alone does not measure job demand, operational suitability, or the future value of learning a tool.

Investigate three separate questions: does the documented abstraction support the intended workload, who maintains the product and its integrations, and can the team operate and recover it? Governance and ecosystem support are useful evidence to seek, but they do not establish why organizations chose a product or whether it meets this team's requirements. Mark those claims unknown until appropriate evidence exists.

**Pause and predict:** if your team finds a tool that is easier than Kubernetes for one narrow deployment path, what would have to be true before you would recommend it for a five-year platform bet?

<details>
<summary>Check your prediction</summary>

Consider the team's required support, security, data recovery, integrations and exit path, then identify which claims can be checked in documentation and which need tests. Multiple providers or contributors may matter to a particular plan, but their number alone cannot prove suitability. State the workload and operating constraints before judging the tool.

</details>

Write the conditions you would require before you continue. The next paragraph is a city-map model. It does not list those conditions.

Think of a platform as a map of dependencies: workloads need paths to storage, network access, recovery and operators who maintain them. The analogy stops at the planning question; a city map cannot establish a product's actual integrations, lifecycle or market adoption. Inspect those facts for the specific version and environment.

Before looking at individual tools, separate four questions. What lifecycle state is documented? Which capabilities does the intended version provide? Which operating requirements remain unverified? What learning or engineering task are you trying to complete? Use those answers to choose the depth of study. Older Swarm material may serve a specific maintenance or comparison task; its age or position beside Compose does not establish relevance. Likewise, dockershim removal alone does not justify abandoning Docker image builds.

## Diagnose Orchestration Dead Ends

Orchestration involves more than starting containers. For a proposed deployment, list the required scheduling, health, rollout, traffic, storage, identity and recovery responsibilities, then check which components actually provide them. A larger ecosystem or a shorter demo does not by itself establish the safer choice for a particular service.

Docker documents swarm mode as part of Docker Engine. To assess it, identify the Engine version and the service, update, networking and failure behavior required by the actual deployment. Comparing a feature with Kubernetes requires documentation for both candidates and a common set of requirements; these sources do not establish comparative adoption or the reasons a team chose either one.

**What it was**: Docker's native orchestration solution.

**Status, checked October 27, 2026**: Docker's [Swarm mode documentation](https://docs.docker.com/engine/swarm/) describes a production runtime built into current Docker Engine versions. It distinguishes Engine swarm mode from Classic Swarm, which is no longer actively developed. That distinction does not establish market share, hiring prospects, or whether Swarm meets a particular team's requirements.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Name[Docker Swarm: identify the product] --> Classic[Classic Swarm: no longer actively developed]
    Name --> Engine[Engine swarm mode: documented production runtime]
    Engine --> Fit[Check capabilities and operating requirements]
```

For either candidate, check who maintains the release, which integrations and support agreements the team depends on, and what happens if that support changes. A governance model is one input to the decision, not proof of competitors' motives or an automatic prediction of integration quality. Record the support questions that remain unanswered.

For this Kubernetes learning route, prioritize the Kubernetes concepts used by the later modules. If work requires Swarm, use documentation for the intended Engine version and inspect its service, networking, update and recovery behavior. A production tutorial is not obsolete merely because it uses Swarm; check its version, requirements and assumptions. Learning priorities for this course are recommendations, not measured career outcomes or evidence that another platform is unusable.

The [Mesos architecture documentation](https://mesos.apache.org/documentation/architecture/) describes a master offering resources to frameworks, whose schedulers choose offers and launch tasks through executors. The [archived Marathon README](https://github.com/d2iq-archive/marathon/blob/90619da70d79a2ecf19368a21c6a695ea981bd74/README.md) describes Marathon as a Mesos framework for container orchestration. This explains the division of responsibilities; it does not establish comparative ease of use or the reasons organizations adopted or left either system.

**What it was**: Two-level resource scheduler (Mesos) with container orchestration (Marathon).

**Status, checked October 27, 2026**: The [Apache Attic record](https://attic.apache.org/projects/mesos.html) identifies Mesos as retired in August 2025, with its Attic move completed in October 2025. This is a formal project-lifecycle fact, rather than a claim that new usage reached zero in an earlier year. Marathon's repository and any distribution support require their own checks; Mesos's status does not establish a separate Marathon retirement date.

```mermaid
timeline
    title Apache Mesos Formal Project Milestones
    2013 : Apache top-level project (June)
    2025 : Project retired (August)
         : Attic move completed (October)
```

For an existing Mesos deployment, identify the frameworks in use, their maintenance arrangements, and how the service handles scheduling, storage, updates and recovery. Apache's retirement record is relevant to an ownership and support plan, but does not establish that a particular installation has failed or that migration is the only defensible decision. Check distribution support independently.

Cloud Foundry's [application deployment guide](https://docs.cloudfoundry.org/devguide/deploy-apps/deploy-app.html) describes deploying applications with `cf push`; its Diego documentation describes Tasks and Long-Running Processes. Those are starting points for assessing a particular distribution, not evidence that all workloads fit or that users migrated for a specific reason. Check version-specific capabilities and the team's required controls before comparing it with another platform.

**What it is**: A platform with documented application deployment workflows and a Diego container management architecture.

**Status, checked October 27, 2026**: [Cloud Foundry's Diego architecture documentation](https://docs.cloudfoundry.org/concepts/diego/diego-architecture.html) describes Diego as the system managing application containers, including scheduling Tasks and Long-Running Processes. This source does not establish the previous blanket claim that Diego was deprecated in favor of Kubernetes. Evaluate the intended distribution, version and workload rather than treating every Cloud Foundry deployment as one lifecycle state.

**Pause and predict:** if a platform serves a web application and a team proposes a new database workload, what evidence would you need before deciding whether to retain or change the platform?

<details>
<summary>Check your prediction</summary>

Name the intended distribution and version, data and recovery requirements, operating ownership, and documented capabilities. Compare those with an alternative using the same criteria and test the unresolved behavior. A new workload suggests questions to investigate; it does not prove a mismatch or explain anyone's migration.

</details>

Write the evidence needed before you continue, including the behavior that has not yet been tested.

The practical diagnosis is to state a possible gap as a hypothesis. Identify the actual requirement and compare it with documentation and observations; a product's historical description does not prove a particular deployment cannot support it.

## Separate Docker Images From the Kubernetes Runtime

Separate the build workflow from the node runtime integration: Kubernetes 1.24 removed the built-in dockershim that connected kubelet to Docker Engine. The precise impact depends on the runtime, build process and workloads in the environment being upgraded.

**What it was**: Dockershim was the built-in integration between kubelet and Docker Engine.

**Status**: Kubernetes removed built-in dockershim in version 1.24; `cri-dockerd` is an external adapter for Docker Engine.

## Define Configuration and Workload Ownership

Configuration management and Kubernetes can address different parts of an operating environment, and their responsibilities can overlap. A team may use configuration management for host settings, cluster provisioning, or Kubernetes API objects. Kubernetes controllers observe state and act to move it toward their desired state. The planning question is which workflow owns each intended change and how that workflow interacts with the controllers managing the workload.

**What they are**: Configuration management and automation tools with capabilities that depend on the product and integration.

**Status**: Evaluate the actual workflow and its ownership boundaries; a tool name alone does not establish a conflict.

| Task | Ownership question |
|------|--------------------|
| Configure a host or provision a cluster | Which automation owns the host settings, and who reviews changes to them? |
| Manage a Kubernetes API object | Which workflow supplies the intended object or fields, and how are changes reviewed? |
| Reconcile a workload | Which Kubernetes controller acts on the desired state, and what does it manage? |
| Coordinate multiple writers | Are their objects or fields deliberately assigned, and how will conflicting changes be resolved? |
| Inspect a node | Which components are involved? Kubernetes documents kubelet and a container runtime on nodes. |

For example, the [Ansible `kubernetes.core.k8s` module](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/collections/kubernetes/core/k8s_module.html), checked October 27, 2026 at collection 6.6.0, uses the Kubernetes API for object creation, reading, updates and deletion. It accepts object definitions; its client-side `apply` option is distinct from `server_side_apply`, which requires `apply: true`. A playbook creating or updating a Pod is not automatically a conflict; identify its owner and subsequent changes. Distinguish a Deployment's desired state from a separate attempt to repair its controller-managed Pods.

The figure is a planning workflow, not a serialized API execution trace. Inspect the write response for conflicts before assuming a requested change was stored; controllers can run concurrently with these inspection steps.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Plan[Agree object and field responsibilities] --> Writer[Automation submits intended API changes]
    Writer --> API[Kubernetes API stores object state]
    API --> Controller[Controller observes and reconciles its workload]
    Controller --> Inspect[Inspect results and ownership conflicts]
    Inspect --> Plan
```

Multiple declarative managers can coexist when their responsibilities are explicit. For example, a team might assign one workflow the application configuration and another a separate operational field. Kubernetes [Server-Side Apply](https://v1-35.docs.kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/server-side-apply/) records field managers and can report a conflict when an apply operation attempts to change a field another manager owns. This mechanism is not a general guarantee that every write or every competing controller will raise a conflict. Inspect the actual write methods and agree how to resolve a disagreement before overriding another manager's claim.

Hypothetical planning example: an Ansible workflow and a GitOps workflow both propose different image values for the same Deployment field. Record which workflow should own the image, which applies it, and how the other workflow will stop asserting a conflicting value. If both use Server-Side Apply, an attempted conflicting change can be rejected; inspect the managers and agree on the intended owner before choosing a resolution. If either uses a different write method, check its behavior rather than assuming the same conflict protection. The example describes a plan, not an observed deployment or a reason to prohibit either tool.

For Compose, distinguish a documented production deployment from an unsupported assumption about availability. Starting several services on one host can meet a bounded deployment need, but a successful local startup does not test recovery after losing that host. Evaluate the data, update and failure requirements of the intended environment. The same requirement check should precede adopting a cluster: adding an orchestrator creates operating responsibilities that also need an owner and verification.

**What it is**: A tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications using a simple YAML file.

**Status, checked October 27, 2026**: Docker explicitly documents [using Compose in production](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/production/), including deployment on a single server and production-specific configuration. A single-host deployment needs an explicit answer for host failure, data recovery, updates, access and monitoring. Production use alone does not establish that Compose is unsuitable, and Kubernetes alone does not establish that those requirements are satisfied.

## Evaluate Technology Bets With Governance, Ecosystem, and Cloud-Provider Signals

When comparing technologies, distinguish a documented lifecycle event from a statement about adoption or the cause of a migration. The supplied records can establish particular statuses and capabilities, but they cannot rank all platforms or explain the decisions of an entire industry. Collect separate evidence for each claim the decision requires.

Keep project lifecycle, capability and decision criteria separate. Apache's Mesos record establishes formal retirement; Docker's Swarm and Compose documentation describes deployment models; Cloud Foundry's documentation explains Diego's architecture. These records do not measure why organizations adopted or left each product. Governance, operating effort and integration requirements are questions for the actual team to investigate, alongside which failure paths its design can tolerate.

| Category | Evidence to collect for the proposed design |
|----------|-----------------|
| Orchestration | Required scheduling, rollout and recovery behavior, plus the components responsible |
| Runtime | Intended versions, CRI conformance and API support; any external adapter and its support |
| Images | Build inputs, target image/workload compatibility and verification results |
| Config | Intended objects and fields, their writers and disagreement handling |
| GitOps | Which desired state the proposed workflow owns and how changes are reviewed |
| Service Mesh | Required traffic or encryption behavior and how the proposed implementation would be tested |
| Monitoring | Required signals, collection paths, alert owners and retention |
| Logging | Required records, collection and access paths, retention and host-loss behavior |

The table prompts an investigation rather than prescribing a product stack. For Kubernetes 1.35, check CRI conformance and the CRI API requirement for the chosen runtime integration. Select image-building, configuration, delivery and observability tools against the team's actual operating needs, support and compatibility evidence.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Product[Identify product and version] --> Record[Read dated maintainer record]
    Record --> Lifecycle[Establish lifecycle and available support]
    Lifecycle --> Requirements[Compare documented capabilities with requirements]
    Requirements --> Test[Test critical operating and recovery paths]
```

Use an evaluation routine whenever a deployment tool appears. Name the problem and required behavior, identify maintainers and relevant support, and inspect version-specific integrations and security responses. Ask how the team would operate or migrate the system if support changed. Record unanswered questions rather than using a star count or a governance label as a substitute for those checks.

Before a pilot, record the operational problem, dependencies, expected result, rollback and evidence needed for the proposed scope. A plugin can also introduce material risk; assess its permissions, failure modes and support instead of assuming that integration is safer than replacement. A faster demo alone does not answer those questions.

A useful distinction is replacement versus integration. Ask which component a proposed change replaces, which interfaces it uses, and which operating responsibilities remain. Cloud Foundry's documented Diego system is one concrete architecture to inspect; do not infer that every distribution has moved to Kubernetes. Likewise, an integration with Kubernetes establishes an interface to evaluate, not proof of why a product succeeded or that a migration is necessary.

Next, examine the Puppet role with care.
